Population of leading American cities (U.S. Bureau of the Census)

| City | 1870 | 1890 |
| New York | 942,292 | 1,515,301 |
| Chicago | 298,977 | 1,099,850 |

Populations are from the decennial census of each year.

source: original; stimulus verified against its source (see source_note)

books.section: Topic 6.8 Immigration and Migration in the Gilded Age
The Rise of the Modern American City

primary_sources: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Population of the 100 Largest Urban Places, 1870 and 1890

stem: Chicago grew from under 300,000 to over 1.1 million in twenty years. Which explanation best fits that growth together with the 1880s immigration surge?

options.text: Chicago’s growth came only from births to families already living there
options.misconception: Explains a quadrupling by births alone, which cannot do it.

options.text: The federal government moved the capital to Chicago in 1880
options.misconception: Invents a move of the capital that never happened.

options.text: Railroads, factories, and immigration drew workers from farms and abroad
Chicago annexed New York and Philadelphia in 1890
options.misconception: Invents an annexation that never happened.

rationales.A: Births alone cannot quadruple a city in twenty years. Newcomers had to arrive.
rationales.B: The capital never moved to Chicago. Washington stayed the capital.
rationales.C: A railroad hub with factories drew farm families and immigrants alike, which is how a city quadruples in twenty years.
rationales.D: Chicago never annexed New York or Philadelphia. They stayed separate cities.
rationales.general:
Ask what could quadruple a city in twenty years.
1. Births alone cannot add 800,000 people that fast.
2. The 1880s brought the largest immigration wave yet.
3. Railroads made Chicago a hub, and its factories needed workers.
4. Farm families and immigrants together supply the growth the numbers show.
Background: the books say mechanization pushed farm families off the land and into cities.
Remember: huge city growth needs newcomers, so look for who moved in.
